title: Black Lives Matter
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher shares stories about Clyde Ross, an African American man who faced numerous challenges, including poverty, racism, and financial exploitation, to highlight the systemic injustices faced by marginalized communities. These experiences demonstrate how historical inequity continues to affect people of color today, often through unfair housing practices and predatory lending. The goal of sharing these stories is not only to educate but also to inspire a deeper understanding of privilege and inequality in American society, encouraging individuals to take action as bodhisattvas to create positive change.

sentences.text: Okay, recording's on.
Let's chant.
*An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma, [unclear: "Israeli met with"] even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the tathagata's words.*
Well, given the situation in our country, I'm taking up a little bit the koan of whiteness, so I don't know, it might delay my completion of the book.
It's been interesting, my initial brief excursions [unclear: "about the frontier"], partly just to feel pretty sort of guilty and embarrassed and ashamed.
I noticed a lot of that, like I should have been investigating this long ago, but now's the moment.
It's always the right moment.

What I wanted to do tonight is share the first part of a long article with you by a journalist named Ta-Nehisi Coates, who writes for The Atlantic magazine and has written several books and is well regarded in these circles, as I understand it.
I'm continuing to get more tips from colleagues at other Soto Zen Buddhist centers through a teacher email list that I'm on.
This article actually explains the details of what the young woman in the video I sent out was saying about monopoly, so if you didn't get a chance to watch that, you might want to.
It's the six-minute video I emailed out by Kimberly Jones, talking about the historic inequity of Black people and how African Americans have been affected by our economic history.
Sometimes you read something and it's the right place and the right time and the right piece, and it really changes your worldview, changes your understanding.
This article has that quality for me.
Maybe it will for you, maybe it won't, and maybe you already know a lot of this.
I also was reflecting about layers of knowing, which is something I think we explore a lot in our practice.

Of course I knew that it was more complicated than the school history told us, that slavery was long ago, and thank you Abraham Lincoln, it's all over now, and it's a mixing pot and we should all be colorblind.
I knew that wasn't true.
But I really didn't get some of the layers and nuances of it, and I'm sure there's a lot more to go.
This is going to be long, so settle in, a little longer than usual for a Dharma talk, even just reading the first few sections of this article.
I'm not sure in the end if we'll have a lot of steam for discussion, but maybe a little.
Mostly I'm hoping to start a conversation, which we kind of started last week with our precept ceremony.
I'll be working with various members, I'm sure, and all of us together, to create educational possibilities for as much as we each need and want.
Our practice can't be removed from this stuff.
Our way is to understand something of wisdom and compassion to empower us as effective bodhisattvas.
And we need to know, I think, a little more about the ground on which we stand as a mostly white community so that we can be those bodhisattvas.
So I better stop introducing it or I really won't have time.
Here is the article, called The Case for Reparations, by Ta-Nehisi Coates.
I'll also post the link to it on The Atlantic and encourage you to read the whole thing.
We'll just put it with the recording once it can get set up.
The Case for Reparations starts with a Bible quote, Deuteronomy 15, 12 to 15.
*If thy brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee and serve thee six years, then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee.
And when thou sendeth him out free from thee, thou shalt not let him go away empty.
Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress.
Furnish him of that wherewith the Lord thy God has blessed thee, thou shalt give unto him.
And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondsman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee.
Therefore I command thee this thing today.*
You need to take care of the slaves when you free them, says the Bible.
*Section one.
Clyde Ross was born in 1923, the seventh of thirteen children, near Clarksdale, Mississippi, the home of the blues.
Ross's parents owned and farmed a forty-acre tract of land, [unclear: "flushed"] with cows, hogs, and mules.
Ross's mother would drive to Clarksdale to do her shopping in a horse and buggy, in which she invested all the pride one might place in a Cadillac.*
*The family owned another horse with a red coat, which they gave to Clyde.
The Ross family wanted for little save that which all black families in the deep south then desperately desired, the protection of the law.
In the 1920s, Jim Crow, Mississippi was, in all facets of society, a kleptocracy.
The majority of the people in the state were perpetually being robbed, robbed of the vote, a hijacking engineered through the trickery of the poll tax and the muscle of the lynch mob.
Between 1882 and 1968, more black people were lynched in Mississippi than any other state.
Quote, you and I know what's the best way to keep a nigger from voting, end quote, blustered Theodore Bilbo, a Mississippi senator and proud Klansman.
You do it the night before the election.*
*The state's regime partnered robbery of the franchise with the robbery of the purse.
Many of Mississippi's black farmers lived in debt peonage under the sway of cotton kings who at once were their landlords, their employers, their primary merchants.
Tools and necessities were advanced against the return on the crop, which was determined by the employer.
When farmers were deemed to be in debt, and they often were, a negative balance was carried over to the next season.
A man or woman who protested this arrangement did so at the risk of grave injury or death.
Refusing to work meant arrest under vagrancy laws and forced labor under the state's penal system.*
*Well into the 20th century, black people spoke of their flight from the Mississippi in much the same way as their renegade ancestors had.
In her 2010 book, [unclear: "The Warmth of Other Sons"], Isabel Wilkerson tells the story of Edie Aravon, a spinach picker who fled Mississippi in 1963 after being made to work at gunpoint. 1963.
You didn't talk about it or tell nobody, Aravon said.
You just had to sneak away.
When Clyde Ross was a child, the Mississippi authorities claimed his father owed $3,000 in back taxes.
The elder Ross could not read.
He did not have a lawyer.
He did not know anyone at the local courthouse.
He could not expect the police to be impartial.
Effectively, the Ross family had no way to contest the claim and no protection under the law.
The authorities seized the land.
They seized the buggy.
They took the cows, hogs, and mules.
And so for the upkeep of separate but equal, the entire Ross family was reduced to sharecropping.
And this was hardly unusual.*
*In 2001, the Associated Press published a three-part investigation into the theft of Black-owned land stretching back to the Antebellum period.
The series documented some 406 victims, and 24,000 acres of land valued at tens of millions of dollars.
The land was taken through means ranging from legal chicanery to terrorism.

Quote, some of the land taken from Black families has now become a country club in Virginia, the AP reported, as well as, quote, oil fields in Mississippi, and, quote, a baseball spring training facility in Florida.*
*Clyde Ross was a smart child.
His teacher thought he should attend a more challenging school.

There was very little support for educating Black people in Mississippi, but Julius Rosenwald, a part owner of Sears Roebuck, had begun an ambitious effort to build schools for Black children throughout the South.
Ross's teacher believed that he should attend the local Rosenwald school.
But it was too far for Ross to walk and get back in time to work in the fields.
Local white children had a school bus.
Clyde Ross did not.
And thus, he lost this chance to better his education.*
*Then when Ross was 10 years old, a group of white men demanded his only childhood possession, the horse with the red coat.
You can't have that horse, we want it, one of the white men said.
They gave Ross's father $17.
I did everything for that horse, Ross told me.
Everything.
Then they took him, put him on a racetrack.
I never did know what happened to him after that, but I know they didn't bring him back.
That's just one of my losses.*
*But the losses only mounted.
As sharecroppers, the Ross family saw their wages treated as landlords' slush fund.
Landowners were supposed to split the profits from the cotton fields with sharecroppers.
But bales would often disappear during the count, or the split might be altered on a whim.
If cotton was selling for 50 cents a pound, the Ross family might get 15 cents or only five.
One year, Ross's mother promised to buy him a $7 suit for a summer program at the church.
She ordered the suit by mail.
But that year, Ross's family was paid only five cents a pound for the cotton.
The mailman arrived with the suit that the Rosses could not pay.
The suit was sent back, and Clyde Ross did not go to the church program.*
*It was in those early years that Ross began to understand himself as an American.
He did not live under the blind decree of justice, but under the heel of a regime that elevated armed robbery to a governing principle.
He thought about fighting.
Just be quiet, his father told him, because they'll come and kill us all.*
*Clyde Ross grew up.
He was drafted into the Army.
The draft officials offered him an exemption if he stayed home and worked.
But he preferred to take his chances with the war.
He was stationed in California, and he found he could go into stores without being bothered.
He could walk the streets without being harassed.
He could go into a restaurant and receive service.
Ross was shipped off to Guam.
He fought in World War II to save the world from tyranny.
But when he returned to Clarksdale, Mississippi, he found that tyranny had followed him home.*
*This was 1947, eight years before Mississippi lynched Everett Till and tossed his broken body into the Tallahatchie River.
And the Great Migration, a mass exodus of seven million African Americans that spanned most of the 20th century, was now in its second wave.
These black pilgrims did not journey north simply to seek better wages and work or to [unclear: "bring or bright lights"] and big adventures.
They were fleeing the acquisitive warlords of the South, and they were seeking the protection of the law.
Clyde Ross was among them.
He came to Chicago in 1947 and took a job as a taster at Campbell's Soup.*
*He made a stable wage.
He married.
He had children.
His paycheck was his own.
No Klansman stripped him of the vote.
When he walked down the street, he did not have to move because of a white man walking past.
He did not have to take off his hat or avert his gaze.
His journey from peonage to full citizenship seemed near complete.
Only one item was missing, a home.
That final badge of entry into the sacred order of the American middle class of the Eisenhower years.
In 1961, Ross and his wife bought a house in North Lonsdale.*
*A bustling community on Chicago's west side, North Lonsdale had long been a predominantly Jewish neighborhood, but a handful of middle class African Americans had lived there starting in the 40s.
The community was anchored by the sprawling Sears Roebuck headquarters.
North Lonsdale's Jewish People's Institute actively encouraged blacks to move into the neighborhood, seeking to make it a pilot community for interracial living.
In the battle for integration then being fought around the country, North Lonsdale seemed to offer promising terrain.
But out in the tall grass, highwaymen, nefarious as any Clarksdale kleptocrat, were lying in wait.*
This was 1961 now.
*Three months after Clyde Ross moved into his house, the boiler blew.
This would normally be a homeowner's responsibility, but in fact Ross was not really a homeowner.
His payments were made to the seller, not to the bank, and Ross had not signed a normal mortgage.
He'd bought On Contract, a predatory agreement that combined all the responsibilities of a home ownership with all the disadvantages of renting, while offering the benefits of neither.
Ross had bought his house for $27,500.
The seller, not the previous homeowner, but a kind of middleman, had bought the house for only $12,000 six months before selling it to Ross.
And in a contract sale, the seller kept the deed until the contract was paid in full.*
*And unlike with a normal mortgage, Ross would acquire no equity in the meantime.
If he missed a single payment, he would immediately forfeit his $1,000 down payment, all his monthly payments, and the property itself.

The men who peddled these contracts in North Lonsdale would sell homes at inflated prices and then evict families who could not pay, taking their down payment and their monthly installments as profit.
Then they'd bring in another black family, rinse and repeat.
Quote, he loads them up with payments they can't meet, an office secretary told the Chicago Daily News of her boss, the speculator Lou Poushanis in 1963.
Then he takes the property away from them.
Why, he sold some of these buildings three or four times.
Ross had tried to get a legitimate mortgage in another neighborhood, but had been told by a loan officer that there was no financing available.*
*The truth was that there was no financing for people like Clyde Ross.
From the 1930s to the 1960s, black people across the country were largely cut off from legitimate home mortgage market through means both legal and extra legal.
Chicago whites employed every measure, from restrictive covenants to bombings to keep their neighborhoods segregated.
And their efforts were buttressed by the federal government.
In 1934, Congress created the Federal Housing Administration.
The FHA insured private mortgages, causing a drop in interest rates and a decline in the size of the down payment required to buy a house, in 1934.
But this insured mortgage was not a possibility for Clyde Ross.
Because the FHA had adopted a system of maps that rated neighborhoods according to their perceived stability.*
*On the maps, green areas rated A, indicating in-demand neighborhoods, as one appraiser put it, because they, quote, they lacked a single foreigner or negro.
These neighborhoods were considered excellent prospects for insurance.
Neighborhoods where black people lived were rated D and were considered ineligible for FHA backing, and they were colored in red.
Neither the percentage of black people living there nor their social class mattered.
Black people were viewed as a contagion.

Redlining went well beyond FHA-backed loans and spread to the entire mortgage industry, which was already rife with racism, including black people from the most legitimate means of obtaining a mortgage.*
*A government offering such bounty to builders and lenders could have required compliance with a non-discrimination policy.

Said Charles Abrams, the urban studies expert who helped create the New York City Housing Authority in 1955, "Instead, the FHA adopted a racial policy that could well have been culled from the Nuremberg laws."
The devastating effects of this are cogently outlined by Melvin L.
Oliver and Thomas M.
Shapiro in their 1995 book, Black Wealth, White Wealth.

Quote from that book: "Locked out of the greatest mass-based opportunity for wealth accumulation in American history, African Americans who desired and were able to afford homeownership found themselves consigned to central city communities where their investments were affected by the self-fulfilling prophecies of these FHA appraisers.
Cut off from sources of new investment, their homes and communities deteriorated and lost value in comparison to those homes and communities that the FHA appraisers deemed desirable."*

*In Chicago and across the country, whites looking to achieve the American dream could rely on a legitimate credit system backed by the government, while blacks were herded into the sights of unscrupulous lenders who took them for money and for sport.
"It was like people who like to go out and shoot lions in Africa.
It was the same thrill," a housing attorney told the historian Beryl Satter in her 2009 book, Family Properties.
"They loved the thrill of the chase and the kill."
And the kill was profitable.*

*At the time of his death, Lou Fuchantis, who owned the note on our case study's house, owned more than 600 properties, many of them in North Lawndale, and his estate was estimated to be worth $3 million.
He'd made much of this money by exploiting the frustrated hopes of black migrants like Clyde Ross.
During that period, according to one estimate, 85% of all black home buyers who bought in Chicago bought on contract.
"If anybody who is well established in this business in Chicago doesn't earn $100,000 a year," a contract seller told the [unclear: "Eve Saturday Evening Post"] in 1962, "he's just loafing."
And so contract sellers became rich and North Lawndale became a ghetto.
Clyde Ross still lives there.
He owns his home.
He is 91, and the emblems of his survival are all around him: awards for service in his community, pictures of his children in cap and gown.
But when I asked him about his home in North Lawndale, I heard only anarchy.
He said, "We were ashamed.
We didn't want anyone to know that we were that ignorant," Ross told me, sitting at his dining room table.
His glasses were as thick as his Clarksdale drawl.
"I come out of Mississippi where there was one mess and come up here and got into another mess.
How dumb am I?
I didn't want anyone to know how dumb I was.
When I found myself caught up in it, I said, 'How?
I just left this mess.
I just left no laws and no regard.'*
*When I came here, I got cheated wide open.
I would probably want to do some harm to some people, you know, if I'd been violent like some of us.
I thought, man, I got caught up in this stuff.
I can't even take care of my kids.
I don't have enough for my kids.
You could fall through the cracks easy, easy, fighting these white people and no law."
And yet fight Ross did.
In 1968, he joined the newly formed Contract Buyers League, a collection of black homeowners on Chicago's south and west side, all of whom had been locked into the same system of predation.*
*There was Howell Collins, whose contract called for him to pay $25,500 for a house a speculator bought for $14,500.

There was Ruth Wells, who managed to pay out half her contract, expecting a mortgage, only to suddenly see an unexpected insurance bill materialize out of thin air, a requirement the seller had added without Wells's knowledge.
Contract sellers used every tool at their disposal to pilfer from their clients.
They scared white residents into selling low.
They lied about properties' compliance with building codes.
They left the buyer responsible when the city inspectors arrived.*
*They presented themselves as real estate brokers when in fact they were the owners.
They guided their clients to lawyers who were in on the scheme.
But the Contract Buyers League fought back.

Members, who would eventually number more than 500, went out to the posh suburbs where the speculators lived and embarrassed them by knocking on their neighbors' doors and informing them of the details of this contract lending trade.
They refused to pay installments, instead holding monthly payments in an escrow account.
They brought a suit against contract sellers, accusing them of buying properties and reselling them in such a manner as to reap from members of the Negro race large and unjust profits.*

*In return for the deprivation of their rights and privileges under the 13th and 14th Amendments, the League demanded, in its prayers for relief, payback of all the monies paid on contract, and all the monies paid for structural improvements of the properties, at 6% interest, minus a fair, non-discriminatory rental price for the time of occupation.
Moreover, the League asked the court to adjudge that the defendants acted willfully and maliciously, and that malice is the gist of this action.
Ross and the Contract Buyers League were no longer appealing to the government simply for equality.
They were no longer fleeing in hopes of a better deal elsewhere.*
*They were charging society with a crime against their community.
They wanted the crime publicly ruled as such.
They wanted the crime's executors declared to be offensive to society.
They wanted restitution for the great injury brought upon them by these offenders.
In 1968, Claude Rice and the Contract Buyers League were no longer simply seeking the protection of the law.
They were seeking reparations.*
Hanging in there, let's do a little bit more.
It's grim, huh?
*According to the most recent statistics, North Lawndale is now on the wrong end of virtually every socioeconomic indicator.
In 1930, its population was 12,000.
Today, it's 36,000.
And the Halcyon talk of interracial living is dead.
The neighborhood is 92% black.
Its homicide rate is 45 per 100,000, triple the rate of the city as a whole.

The infant mortality rate is 14 per thousand, twice the national average. 43% of the people in North Lawndale live in poverty, double Chicago's overall rate. 45% of all households are on food stamps, three times the rate of the city at large.
Sears Roebuck left the neighborhood in 1987, taking 1,800 jobs with it.
Kids in North Lawndale need not be confused about their prospects either.
Cook County's juvenile detention center sits directly in the neighborhood.*
*North Lawndale is an extreme portrait of the trends that [unclear: "ale"] black Chicago.
Such is the magnitude of these ailments that it can be said that blacks and whites do not inhabit the same city.
The average per capita income of Chicago's white neighborhoods is almost three times that of its black neighborhoods.

When the Harvard sociologist Robert Sampson examined incarceration rates in Chicago in his 2012 book, Great American City, he found that a black neighborhood with one of the highest incarceration rates had a rate more than 40 times as high as the white neighborhood with the highest rate in white neighborhoods.
"This is a staggering differential, even for a community level comparison," Sampson writes.
"A difference of kind, not of degree."
In other words, Chicago's impoverished black neighborhoods, characterized by high unemployment and households headed by single parents, are not simply poor.
They are ecologically distinct.
"This is not simply the same thing as low economic status," writes Sampson.
And in this pattern, Chicago is not alone.*
*The lives of black Americans are better than they were half a century ago.
The humiliation of whites-only signs is gone.
Rates of black poverty have decreased.
Black teen pregnancy rates are at record lows, and the gap between black and white teen pregnancy rates has also shrunk.
But such progress rests on a shaky foundation, and fault lines are everywhere.
The income gap between black and white households is roughly the same today as it was in 1970.
Patrick Sharkey, a sociologist at New York University, studied children born from 1955 through 1970 and found that 4% of whites and 62% of blacks were raised in poor neighborhoods.*
*A generation later, the same study showed virtually nothing has changed.
And whereas whites born into affluent neighborhoods tend to remain in affluent neighborhoods, blacks tend to fall out of them.
This is not surprising.
Black families, regardless of income, are significantly less wealthy than white families.
The Pew Research Center estimates that white households are worth roughly 20 times as much as black households.
And whereas only 15% of whites have zero or negative wealth, more than a third of blacks do.
Effectively, the black family in America is working without a safety net.
When financial calamity strikes, a [unclear: "metal"] emergency, divorce, job loss, the fall is precipitous.*
*And just as black families of all incomes remain handicapped by lack of wealth, so too they remain handicapped by their restricted choice of neighborhood.
Black people with upper middle class incomes do not generally live in upper middle class neighborhoods.
Sharkey's research also shows that black families making $100,000 typically live in the kind of neighborhoods inhabited by white families making $30,000.
"Blacks and whites inhabit different neighborhoods," Sharkey writes.
But this is not possible.
So such different neighborhoods that it's not possible to compare the economic outcomes of black and white children, just in different worlds.*
Skip a little bit and then here's the outcome on the Contract Buyers League.
*The Contract Buyers League suit brought by Clyde Ross and his allies took direct aim at this inheritance.
The suit had roots in Chicago's long history of segregation, which had created these two housing markets: one legitimate and backed by the government, the other lawless and patrolled by predators.
The suit dragged on and on until 1976, when the League lost a jury trial.
Securing the equal protection of the law proved hard.
Securing reparations proved impossible.

If there were any doubts about the mood of the jury, the foreman removed them by saying, when asked about the verdict, that he hoped it would end, quote, "the mess Earl Warren made with this Brown versus Board of Education nonsense."
And the Supreme Court seemed to share that sentiment.*
*The past two decades have witnessed a rollback of the progressive legislation of the 1960s.
Liberals have found themselves on the defensive.
In 2008, when Barack Obama was a candidate for president, he was asked whether his daughters, Malia and Sasha, should benefit from affirmative action.
He answered in the negative.
But this exchange rested on an erroneous comparison: a comparison of the average American white family with an exceptional first family.
In the contest of upward mobility, Barack and Michelle Obama had won.
But they won by being twice as good and enduring twice as much.
Malia and Sasha Obama enjoy privileges beyond the average White House dreams.
But the comparison is incomplete.
The more telling question is how would they compare with Jenna and Barbara Bush, the products of many generations of privilege, not just one.
Whatever the Obama children achieve will be evidence of their family's singular perseverance and not of broad equality.*
So I think I'll stop there.
It's just such a long and in-depth article.

And we do go back a little later to more about the story of Clyde Ross and his life and how he did manage to finish paying this contract on his house by working three jobs and not being there for his family, and the people who did survive that system, and something about the many others who didn't.
And then he does a much deeper dive, even deeper than that, into all the historical facts and figures of how all the system came to be.
So: Black Lives Matter, clearly.
And I was thinking about this in my family and realizing there's a lot I don't know.
My mom's family was very middle class and working White.
My grandmother lived in a trailer home, which she did own, and my mom's aunt and uncle owned a small chicken farm, which they did own.
It was just a chicken farm.
But they had, from generations previously, clearly been able to get on this wealth engine of ownership, which Black Americans were excluded from.
And he also gives lots of facts and figures about just the overall incredible economic impact of slavery.
And that's really worth reading.

So I really recommend this article: the early and even later economies of the United States are completely and powerfully empowered by free and cheap labor, and the slavery industry itself was a powerful generator of wealth for White people, buying and selling and breeding slaves.
So it's a grim picture, that's for sure.
But it just shifted me out of that frame of, like, well, I know I'm privileged.
I know I have advantages.
And some of my best friends are Black, in that whole frame.
And I just realized this is a much, much deeper thing than this.
This is a massive, massive setup going back hundreds and hundreds of years.
And it's crazy now to not think that something hugely massive needs to change if it's ever to be corrected.
And so this article talks about that, too.
It talks about possibilities for reparations and change.
And the other thing that's just starting to shift in me is the idea that African Americans are sort of just one of a bunch of minorities, which are all more or less the same thing.
But that's clearly not the case either.
And of course, there are other minority groups who suffered horrible injustices.
And here we think right away of Native Americans as well.

But there are certain ways, and he makes a powerful argument for this in this article, and I'm curious to read other books and learn more, that the African American experience is really unique, and really was engineered in a powerful way to lead with certainty to incredible inequity that persists to today.
So thank you for listening to all that.
I don't know if there's anything to say now or if we should just digest.
And, again, maybe you know more about this than I do.
So I just happened to have the bully pulpit, so I used it.
Maybe we should actually just sit in silence for a minute and [unclear: "enchant"].
Would that be a good plan?
OK.
Yeah, I know.
What words are there for this?
